per_case.playbook: Tune/suppress the FLOW-002 high-count heuristic for internal-to-internal web service traffic; baseline expected flow volume for 192.168.100.46 -> 192.168.100.5:80 and confirm with the app owner that bulk HTTP transfers are expected. No containment required.

1) Immediately isolate 192.168.100.5 at the switch/VLAN level (do not power off - preserve volatile state). 2) Block all traffic to/from .5, especially 100.3:0 and 100.46:80/3456. 3) Acquire memory and disk images from .5 for C2 implant/malware analysis and pull its beacon config, intervals, and payloads to identify controller logic. 4) Treat 192.168.100.46, .147, .148, .149, .150 as potentially infected fleet - run EDR/AV sweep, inspect for scheduled tasks, beacons, and persistence on each. 5) Reset all credentials cached or used on .5 and audit authentication logs for lateral movement. 6) Enable full packet capture and flow logging (endpoint_events and firewall_events are currently empty) to restore visibility and validate containment. 7) Escalate to IR and, if exfiltration is confirmed, initiate data-loss assessment for anything routed through 100.3.

1) Isolate 192.168.100.55 from the network segment per containment policy, preserving an evidence capture of the active session pairs. 2) Pull process/Bot-IoT agent inventory and running-process hashes from the host to identify the process generating the 'BOTIOT-' session pattern. 3) Scrutinize the counterpart 192.168.100.3 for listener behavior on 8080 and for the same agent, since traffic is reciprocal. 4) Review host egress baselines and confirm no external C2 destinations were contacted from either endpoint. 5) Suppress or retune FLOW-002 on port 80/8080 for these internal pairs once the automation is identified, since the detection is misfiring on large mirrored bulk transfers rather than brute force. 6) Reconstruct timeline around the alert to determine if the 59 sessions represent legitimate backup/telemetry or a hijacked IoT device in a botnet peer-to-peer loop. 7) No perimeter block is required; escalate to host-IR team for containment and root-cause.

No containment action. Suppress/tune the FLOW-005 'beacon receiver' signature for internal-to-internal TCP/80 service traffic with bidirectional responses so it does not flag internal web servers. Record 192.168.100.7 as an internal HTTP server and whitelist its 3 known client hosts. Optionally verify with the platform owner that the UDP/565 stream to 192.168.100.3 is an approved telemetry collector; monitor only, do not block.

Block 162.208.20.178 at perimeter egress/ingress (both 80 and 443) and add to deny lists; hunt and contain beaconing on all six originating internal hosts (192.168.10.5 first, then .8, .9, .15, .12, .25) via host isolation and memory/AV sweep for implant persistence; capture packet evidence of the beacon template (334/3776 and 1168/4356 byte payloads) for signature creation; review DNS/hostname resolution records for the C2 domain; monitor for re-beaconing to alternate C2 IPs after the block.

Block 178.255.83.1 (all ports) at the perimeter and proxy egress-denylist; confirm the block and verify beacon cessation on the 12 internal sources; pull DNS/proxy logs for 178.255.83.1 and any sibling C2 infrastructure; submit the two beacon flow archetypes (438/860-byte 5-packet sessions and 0-byte 4-packet sessions) as IDS signatures; then perform host triage (autoruns, scheduled tasks, browser/agent artifacts, memory) on 192.168.10.16, .9, .14, and .12 as highest-volume beacons and escalate to host isolation if a payload or persistence mechanism is found.
No action / close alert. Optionally baseline-normalize DNS query volume from 192.168.10.3 to prevent future false positives on high-count resolver traffic.

Close FLOW-005 as a false positive (direction-blind signature) and downgrade FLOW-002 as benign high-volume DNS. Take no host action on 192.168.10.14 - do not isolate and do not block, since it is the victim of the scan, not the actor. Separately open/prioritize an investigation into 192.168.10.8, which produced a 1000-flow, 745-port sweep with near-zero responses against 192.168.10.14; tune the FLOW-005 signature to require the internal source host to be a repeated initiator of uniform small flows rather than any flow where the external/internal peer sits in the dest field.

Close the FLOW-002 alert on 192.168.10.15 as a false positive (suppress/tune the port-53 flow-count signature with a higher threshold and a resolver allowlist for 192.168.10.3). Separately open a NEW high-priority case against 192.168.10.8 for internal port scanning: pull full packet capture and endpoint telemetry for the two scan windows (t=618-627s, t=2299-2309s), identify the 569 probed ports' services, review .8's process/authentication history for malware or an unattended scanner, and isolate 192.168.10.8 if unauthorized scanning is confirmed. Additionally verify 192.168.10.15's DNS-query signature against its EDR telemetry to rule out a DNS-tunneling client before fully closing.

1) Block 205.174.165.73 inbound and outbound at the perimeter and all egress points. 2) Isolate and forensic-triage the beaconing hosts in priority order: 192.168.10.25 (exfil volume), 192.168.10.8, then .15/.14/.9/.5. 3) Hunt all six hosts for persistence, scheduled tasks and non-standard-port (444/8080) processes, and pull full packet captures for the port-444 sessions. 4) Assess exfiltration scope for 192.168.10.25 (~12.9 MB uploaded) and force credential resets for any account active on the affected machines. 5) Add proactive detections for repeated 1-packet/0-byte flows to a single external peer and for asymmetric uploads to non-standard ports. 6) Re-run threat-intel enrichment on 205.174.165.73 once an AbuseIPDB key is available and share IOCs with peers.

1) Block 23.50.75.27 at the egress firewall and DNS/proxy layer (any port, prioritize 80/TCP) and log all denied attempts. 2) Threat-hunt the 11 internal sources (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .12, .14, .15, .16, .17, .19, .25, .51) for beaconing persistence: scheduled tasks, services, browser/proxy artifacts, and any process resolving or connecting to the IP. 3) Pull full proxy/Zeek session logs for these hosts to identify the user-agents and URIs used in the ~1.77KB responses. 4) Quarantine/reset sessions and collect memory images from the highest-volume talkers (192.168.10.8, .14, .16) first. 5) If a specific host is later confirmed compromised, escalate that host to isolation. 6) Re-ingest and re-verify for any new external peers after the block.

Triage/Close - False Positive from Volumetric Flow Alert: verify no endpoint detections on the 12 internal hosts, confirm port-80-only peer concentration is a known/shared web service, document low-payload variance vs. beacon cadence, tune FLOW-005 threshold, and monitor 23.61.187.27 for any change in flow regularity or payload uniformity before escalating.

1) Block 72.167.239.239 at the perimeter firewall and sinkhole DNS for any resolved domains. 2) Block TCP/80 egress to this IP and alert on any further attempts. 3) Immediately hunt and isolate the 11 internal hosts (192.168.10.5/.8/.9/.12/.14/.15/.16/.17/.19/.25/.51) — capture memory, pull EDR telemetry, and reset credentials, as all show exclusive beacon traffic to the C2 with no benign network baseline. 4) Perform PCAP review of a sample of uniform 2267-byte callback pairs to extract the C2 protocol pattern and check for additional receiver IPs. 5) Add a detection rule for low-diversity internal hosts contacting a single external peer across the full capture window.

1) Block 72.21.91.29 bidirectionally at the perimeter firewall/proxy and add it to a DNS-sinkhole/blocklist. 2) Pull full-session PCAP/HTTP Host headers for TCP/80 traffic to this IP to identify the exact URI/process pattern. 3) Sweep the 13 participating internal hosts (192.168.10.16, .12, .8, .14, .15, .9, .5, .17, .51, .19, .50, .25, .3) for the beaconing process, scheduled tasks, and persistence; deploy EDR hunting for the fixed 437/796-byte request template. 4) Search for alternate C2 peers (same payload template, other destination IPs) to detect failover. 5) If any single host is confirmed compromised, escalate that host to isolation; keep perimeter block on the external IP.
